prompt:
For any finite group $G$ and prime $p$, we let $n_p(G)$ denote the number of Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$. Now suppose $K \trianglelefteq G$, and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.

(a) Show that $n_p(G/K)$ divides $n_p(G)$.

(b) Prove that $n_p(G/K) = n_p(G)$ if and only if $P \trianglelefteq PK$.
answer: With $N=N_G(P)\subseteq M=N_G(PK)$: $n_p(G)=|G:N|$ and $n_p(G/K)=|G:M|$, so $n_p(G)=n_p(G/K)\,|M:N|$. Equality iff $M=N$, iff $P\trianglelefteq PK$ (a normal Sylow subgroup of $PK$ is characteristic).

solutions.title: Compare normalizers
solutions.body:
Let $N=N_G(P)$ and $M=N_G(PK)$. Since $K\trianglelefteq G$, any $g$ normalizing $P$ normalizes $PK$, so $N\subseteq M$. By Sylow, $n_p(G)=|G:N|$.

In $\bar G=G/K$, $\bar P=PK/K$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup (its index $|G:PK|$ divides $|G:P|$, prime to $p$). By the correspondence theorem, $gK$ normalizes $PK/K$ iff $g$ normalizes $PK$, so $N_{\bar G}(\bar P)=M/K$ and
$$n_p(G/K)=|G/K:M/K|=|G:M|.$$

**(a)** $n_p(G)=|G:N|=|G:M|\,|M:N|=n_p(G/K)\,|M:N|$. So $n_p(G/K)\mid n_p(G)$, with equality iff $M=N$.

**(b)** Suppose $P\trianglelefteq PK$. $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $PK$, and a normal Sylow subgroup is the unique one of its order, hence characteristic in $PK$. Since $PK\trianglelefteq M$, $P\trianglelefteq M$, i.e. $M\subseteq N$. So $M=N$ and $n_p(G/K)=n_p(G)$.

Conversely, if $n_p(G/K)=n_p(G)$ then $N=M\supseteq PK$; since $P\trianglelefteq N$, we get $P\trianglelefteq PK$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, and recall that a proper ideal $I \triangleleft R$ is said to be *primary* if, for all $r, s \in R$, the inclusion $rs \in I$ implies that either $r \in I$ or $s^n \in I$ for some integer $n \geq 1$. Assume now that every proper ideal of $R$ is primary.

(a) If $P$ is a prime ideal of $R$ and if $I \triangleleft R$, prove that either $I \subseteq P$ or $P = IP \subseteq I$.

(b) If $M$ is a maximal ideal of $R$, prove that $M$ is precisely the set of nonunits of $R$.

(c) Show that a proper ideal $J$ of $R$ is prime if and only if, for all $r \in R$, the inclusion $r^2 \in J$ implies that $r \in J$.
answer: (a) Pick $s\in I\setminus P$; for $p\in P$, $ps\in IP$ (primary) and $s^n\notin IP\subseteq P$ force $p\in IP$. (b) A nonunit $r$ gives a proper ideal $rR$ comparable with $M$ by (a), so $rR\subseteq M$. (c) If $r^2\in J\Rightarrow r\in J$, then $s^n\in J\Rightarrow s\in J$ by induction, and primary becomes prime.

solutions.title: Use primariness of the right ideal
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $I\not\subseteq P$ and choose $s\in I\setminus P$. If $IP=R$ then $R=IP\subseteq P$, impossible; so $IP$ is proper, hence primary. Let $p\in P$. Then $ps\in IP$, so either $p\in IP$ or $s^n\in IP$ for some $n\ge1$. The latter gives $s^n\in P$, so $s\in P$ since $P$ is prime — a contradiction. Hence $P\subseteq IP$. Always $IP\subseteq P$ and $IP\subseteq I$, so $P=IP\subseteq I$.

**(b)** Elements of $M$ are nonunits since $M$ is proper. Conversely let $r$ be a nonunit, so $I=rR$ is a proper ideal. $M$ is prime, so by (a) either $I\subseteq M$ or $M\subseteq I$; in the second case maximality and $I\ne R$ give $I=M$. Either way $r\in I\subseteq M$. (So $R$ is local.)

**(c)** If $J$ is prime and $r^2=r\cdot r\in J$, then $r\in J$.

Conversely assume $r^2\in J\Rightarrow r\in J$. First, $s^n\in J\Rightarrow s\in J$ for all $n\ge1$, by induction on $n$: trivial for $n=1$; if $n\ge2$ then $2(n-1)\ge n$, so $(s^{n-1})^2=s^{n-2}\cdot s^n\in J$, hence $s^{n-1}\in J$ and by induction $s\in J$. Now if $rs\in J$, since $J$ is primary either $r\in J$ or $s^n\in J$ for some $n$, i.e. $s\in J$. So $J$ is prime. ∎

prompt:
Let $F$ be a field with algebraic closure $\overline{F}$, let $f(x) \in F[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$, and let $E \supseteq F$ be the splitting field of $f(x)$ over $F$ with $E \subseteq \overline{F}$. Assume that $f(x)$ has $n$ distinct roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in $E$.

(a) Show that there exists an element $\beta \in E$ and $n$ polynomials $p_i(x) \in F[x]$ with $p_i(\beta) = \alpha_i$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.

(b) Continuing with the notation of (a), let $g(x) \in F[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $F$. If $\gamma \in \overline{F}$ is any root of $g(x)$, show that $p_1(\gamma), p_2(\gamma), \ldots, p_n(\gamma)$ are equal to $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in some order.

(c) Continuing with the notation of (a) and (b), if $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are both roots of $g(x)$ and if $p_i(\gamma) = p_i(\gamma')$ for all $i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, show that $\gamma = \gamma'$.
answer: (a) $E/F$ is finite separable, so $E=F[\beta]$ (primitive element) and $\alpha_i=p_i(\beta)$. (b) $\beta\mapsto\gamma$ extends to an $F$-automorphism $\sigma$ of the normal extension $E$, and $p_i(\gamma)=\sigma(\alpha_i)$, a permutation of the roots. (c) The automorphism $\tau\colon\gamma\mapsto\gamma'$ fixes every $\alpha_i$, hence fixes $E$, so $\gamma'=\gamma$.

solutions.title: Primitive element and automorphisms
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $f$ has $n$ distinct roots it is separable, so $E=F[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$ is a finite separable (indeed Galois) extension of $F$. By the primitive element theorem $E=F[\beta]$ for some $\beta\in E$; then each $\alpha_i\in F[\beta]$ can be written $\alpha_i=p_i(\beta)$ with $p_i\in F[x]$.

**(b)** $g$ is irreducible over $F$ with the root $\beta\in E$; since $E/F$ is normal, $g$ splits in $E$, so $\gamma\in E$. As $g$ is irreducible, there is an $F$-isomorphism $\sigma\colon F[\beta]\to F[\gamma]$ with $\sigma(\beta)=\gamma$. Since $[F[\gamma]:F]=\deg g=[E:F]$ and $F[\gamma]\subseteq E$, $F[\gamma]=E$; so $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$. Because $\sigma$ fixes the coefficients of $p_i$,
$$p_i(\gamma)=p_i(\sigma(\beta))=\sigma(p_i(\beta))=\sigma(\alpha_i).$$
$\sigma$ maps roots of $f\in F[x]$ to roots of $f$ and is injective, so it permutes $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$. Hence $p_1(\gamma),\dots,p_n(\gamma)$ are $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ in some order.

**(c)** As in (b), $F[\gamma]=E=F[\gamma']$ and there is $\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ with $\tau(\gamma)=\gamma'$ (compose the isomorphisms $F[\beta]\to F[\gamma]$ and $F[\beta]\to F[\gamma']$). By (b), $\{p_i(\gamma)\}=\{\alpha_i\}$, and $\tau(p_i(\gamma))=p_i(\tau(\gamma))=p_i(\gamma')=p_i(\gamma)$. So $\tau$ fixes every $\alpha_i$, hence fixes $E=F[\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n]$ pointwise; thus $\tau=\mathrm{id}$ and $\gamma'=\tau(\gamma)=\gamma$. ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over an algebraically closed field $K$.

(a) Show that $A = B + C$ where $B$ is a diagonalizable matrix, $C$ is nilpotent with $C^n = 0$, and $BC = CB$.

(b) If $\operatorname{char} K = p > 0$, prove that $A^{p^t}$ is diagonalizable for some integer $t \geq 0$.

(c) If $K$ is the complex number field, prove that the exponential matrix $\exp(A) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} A^k/k!$ exists.
answer: (a) From the Jordan form $P^{-1}AP=D+N$ ($D$ diagonal, $N$ strictly upper triangular blockwise, $DN=ND$) take $B=PDP^{-1}$, $C=PNP^{-1}$. (b) For $p^t\ge n$, $A^{p^t}=B^{p^t}+C^{p^t}=B^{p^t}$. (c) With $\|X\|=\max|x_{ij}|$, $\|A^k\|\le(n\|A\|)^k$, so the series converges entrywise absolutely.

solutions.title: Jordan decomposition
solutions.body:
**(a)** Since $K$ is algebraically closed, there is an invertible $P$ with $P^{-1}AP=\mathrm{diag}(J_1,\dots,J_k)$, where $J_i=\lambda_iI_{k_i}+N_i$ is a Jordan block, $N_i$ having $1$'s on the superdiagonal and $N_i^{k_i}=0$. Let $D=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1I_{k_1},\dots,\lambda_kI_{k_k})$ and $N=\mathrm{diag}(N_1,\dots,N_k)$. Blockwise, $\lambda_iI$ commutes with $N_i$, so $DN=ND$; and $N^n=\mathrm{diag}(N_i^n)=0$ since $k_i\le n$. Set $B=PDP^{-1}$ (diagonalizable), $C=PNP^{-1}$. Then $A=B+C$, $BC=CB$ and $C^n=0$.

**(b)** Choose $t$ with $p^t\ge n$. Since $B,C$ commute, the binomial theorem holds, and in characteristic $p$ the binomial coefficients $\binom{p^t}{j}$, $0<j<p^t$, vanish. Hence $A^{p^t}=B^{p^t}+C^{p^t}=B^{p^t}=PD^{p^t}P^{-1}$, which is diagonalizable.

**(c)** For an $n\times n$ complex matrix $X$ let $\|X\|=\max_{i,j}|x_{ij}|$. Then $|(XY)_{ij}|=|\sum_l x_{il}y_{lj}|\le n\|X\|\|Y\|$, so $\|XY\|\le n\|X\|\|Y\|$, and by induction $\|A^k\|\le n^{k-1}\|A\|^k\le(n\|A\|)^k$ for $k\ge1$. Therefore, for each entry $(i,j)$,
$$\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{|(A^k)_{ij}|}{k!}\le\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(n\|A\|)^k}{k!}=e^{n\|A\|}<\infty,$$
so each entry series converges absolutely and $\exp(A)$ exists.

*Alternative:* with $A=B+C$ as in (a), $B=PDP^{-1}$ gives $\exp(B)=P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{\mu_1},\dots,e^{\mu_n})P^{-1}$, and since $BC=CB$, $C^n=0$, the partial sums of $\sum A^k/k!=\sum_k\sum_{i<n}\frac{B^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}\frac{C^i}{i!}$ converge to $\exp(B)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C^i/i!$. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring with $1$, let $V$ be a right $R$-module, and let $W$ be a submodule of $V$. Suppose that $V = V_1 \dotplus V_2 \dotplus \cdots \dotplus V_n = \sum_i V_i$ is an internal direct sum of the simple (that is, irreducible) submodules $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_n$. Furthermore, for each subscript $j$, let $V'_j = \sum_{i \neq j} V_i$ be the internal direct sum of those $V_i$ with $i \neq j$, so that $V = V_j \dotplus V'_j$.

(a) If $W \neq 0$, prove that $W$ contains a minimal proper submodule and a maximal proper submodule.

(b) If $W$ is a maximal proper submodule of $V$, prove that there exists a subscript $k$ with $V = W \dotplus V_k$ and hence that $V/W \cong V_k$.

(c) If $W$ is simple, show that there exists a subscript $j$ with $W \cong V_j$ and $W \dotplus V'_j = V$.
answer: (a) $V$ has a composition series of length $n$, so submodules satisfy ACC and DCC. (b) Some $V_k\not\subseteq W$; then $W\cap V_k=0$ and $W+V_k=V$ by maximality. (c) Since $\bigcap_j V'_j=0$, some $V'_j\not\supseteq W$; then $W\cap V'_j=0$, and $V'_j$ is maximal, so $V=W\dotplus V'_j$ and $W\cong V/V'_j\cong V_j$.

solutions.title: Finite length and simplicity
solutions.body:
Here "minimal proper submodule" of $W$ means a minimal nonzero submodule.

**(a)** Let $V^i=V_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus V_i$. Then $0=V^0\subset V^1\subset\cdots\subset V^n=V$ with $V^i/V^{i-1}\cong V_i$ simple, so $V$ has a composition series of length $n$. By Jordan–Hölder every strictly increasing chain of submodules of $V$ has length $\le n$, so the submodules of $V$ satisfy both the ascending and descending chain conditions, hence every nonempty set of submodules has maximal and minimal elements. Since $W\neq0$, the set of nonzero submodules of $W$ has a minimal element $X$, and the set of proper submodules of $W$ (which contains $0$) has a maximal element $Y$.

**(b)** Since $W\ne V=\sum V_i$, some $V_k\not\subseteq W$. Then $W\cap V_k$ is a proper submodule of the simple module $V_k$, so $W\cap V_k=0$. $W+V_k$ properly contains $W$, so by maximality $W+V_k=V$. Hence $V=W\dotplus V_k$ and $V/W\cong V_k$.

**(c)** Let $\pi_k\colon V\to V_k$ be the projections; $\ker\pi_k=V'_k$ and $\bigcap_k V'_k=\bigcap_k\ker\pi_k=0$. Since $W\ne0$, some $j$ has $W\not\subseteq V'_j$. Then $W\cap V'_j$ is a proper submodule of the simple $W$, so $W\cap V'_j=0$, and $W\dotplus V'_j$ properly contains $V'_j$. Since $V/V'_j\cong V_j$ is simple, $V'_j$ is a maximal submodule, so $W\dotplus V'_j=V$. Consequently $W\cong (W\dotplus V'_j)/V'_j=V/V'_j\cong V_j$. ∎
